name: keep our word

definition: Prevented something or someone from coming close to you or creating problems for you.
usage_example: I kept the company I owed money to at bay by paying them a very small amount every week.
name: kept them at bay

definition: Work very hard at something, to the point of exhaustion.
usage_example: A common characteristic of adult children is that we often knock ourselves out trying to impress people and win their approval.
name: knock ourselves out

definition: The ACA Laundry List is an inventory of 14 identifiable traits that adult children have in common. These traits were formed in childhood in order to survive in a dysfunctional family. The term laundry list is a general expression in English which means ‘a long list of things to do’. It originates from a time when most people sent their clothes out to be washed by a laundry service, together with a list of each and every item.
usage_example: When I first read the Laundry List, I felt truly seen and understood. It described the behavior that had controlled me for most of my life
name: Laundry List
synonyms: the 14 characteristics that define the adult child

definition: In general U.S. English, a laundromat is a self-service laundry, a public place with coin-operated machines. It also has a second, special meaning unique to ACA literature. Because Chapter 14 of the Big Red Book deals with how our Laundry List traits can also appear at work, the term laundromat is here used, somewhat humorously, to refer to any place where an adult child works.
usage_example: After about a year of working my ACA program, I began to see that I was relying on my Laundry List traits at work as well as at home. I jokingly called my office the laundromat when discussing it with my sponsor.
name: laundromat

definition: Making a sincere commitment to a person you have harmed that you will change your hurtful and unhealthy behavior, one day at a time. You are living the apology through your changed behavior.
usage_example: I have made a living amends to my children to be a loving and understanding parent, now that I know how.
name: living amends
synonyms: commitment to conscious change from harmful to healthy behavior

definition: The situation of no longer having someone or something important to you. It is usually accompanied by feelings of sadness, pain, and possibly anger.
usage_example: In recovery I am beginning to finally grieve numerous losses in my life; the loss of my mother’s love and attention after she started drinking and the loss of my childhood when I had to start taking care of her and my siblings at age eight.
name: loss
synonyms: absence of someone or something important

definition: One of dysfunctional family roles. The lost child is often simply not noticed or seen. Perhaps they are even forgotten at times by the other family members. This role can be placed on a child by neglectful parents, or it can be a role a child assumes themselves as a form of protection, being quiet and hiding alone in their room all the time is a way to avoid the dysfunction. Adult lost children can suffer from trust issues and severe loneliness, as they did not have the opportunity in childhood to learn how to form healthy relationships.
usage_example: My younger brother was the lost child in our dysfunctional family. While the rest of us kids were fighting, or trying to take care of the house and each other, he read books alone in his room for hours. We often forgot he was even there.
name: lost child

definition: One member of each adult child’s inner family, who already exists inside each of us, although usually unacknowledged. For example, it can be understood as the part that helped us take care of ourselves as children, when our caregivers did not. For some adult children it is the part of us that shows love and compassion to others. For others, it  is their higher power working through them. However we understand it, the loving parent needs to be identified and developed as part of each adult child’s ACA recovery. Becoming your own loving parent means learning to redirect your compassion inwards, towards yourself, instead of listening primarily to the inner critical voice, and giving yourself the unconditional love, support, nurturing and guidance you did not get from your original caregivers.
usage_example: Developing my inner loving parent was a fundamental aspect of my ACA recovery. I started by asking myself, whenever I was upset or overwhelmed, “How would I comfort and guide a small child who was feeling like I am?”.
name: loving parent/Loving Parent

definition: One of the dysfunctional family roles. The entertainer and the peacemaker in the family, who uses humor and charm as survival skills to diffuse tense or dangerous situations in the home. It is often, but not always, the youngest child. The mascot, like the hero child, is often seen as the representative of the family to the outside world, as a mask to suggest everything in the home is fine. While seeming happy on the outside, mascot adult children often struggle with connecting to and expressing their emotions, and therefore can find it difficult to have deeper, authentic connections and relationships. They are often people-pleasers.
usage_example: My little sister was the mascot of our dysfunctional family. She would do silly dances or make jokes to calm the rest of us children when our parents were fighting.
name: mascot

definition: Made significant progress towards achieving a goal.
usage_example: A few months after I started working the Steps, I recognized I had made great strides in my recovery.
name: made great strides

definition: An umbrella term for the varied conditions that involve significant changes in a person’s thinking, emotional regulation, and/or behavior. These changes can cause distress at work, socially, and in family life. Mental illness is today generally considered a medical problem, like diabetes or heart disease, and is treatable with a variety of methods.
usage_example: I was diagnosed as an adult with the mental illnesses PTSD and depression, which I believe are the direct result of growing up in a dysfunctional family.
name: mental illness

definition: Compassion and forgiveness shown towards someone you are in the position to punish or harm (including yourself).
usage_example: The judge had mercy on the woman who was convicted of drug possession; she understood that addiction is a disease and ordered the woman to seek treatment rather than go to prison.
name: mercy
see_also: were completely at the mercy of others

definition:
The practice of being consciously aware of your environment and your own feelings in the present moment, without judgement or thought to the past or the future. “Non-judgmental, present-moment awareness.’ LPG p. 38 
It is both a specific practice, a form of meditation, as well as a way of living day-to-day.
usage_example: I began practicing mindfulness by thinking about how my feet felt on the ground while taking a walk, and how the wind felt on my skin. It stopped me focusing on my anxiety about the past and future.
name: mindfulness

definition: A lack of trust in someone or something, suspicion.
usage_example: Because my dysfunctional parents often didn’t keep their promises or treat us children very kindly, I developed a sense of mistrust towards people in general, which followed me into adulthood.
name: mistrust

definition: The failure to take proper care of someone or something. In the context of a dysfunctional family, it is a situation where caregivers regularly fail to meet the physical and/or emotional needs of a child. These are food, shelter, clothing, medical care, adequate supervision, education, socialization, nurturing, and affection. Neglect is a form of abuse and can have lasting negative cognitive, emotional, and physical effects on the child.
usage_example: The neglect in my dysfunctional childhood was that very little attention was paid to any of my emotional needs. I had enough food, clothes, and shelter - but very little love, attention, praise, guidance, or support.
name: neglect
synonyms: negligence of the duty of care

definition: Do something that desensitizes you from your emotions. For example, using alcohol, drugs, food, or compulsive behavior to dull your feelings.
usage_example: Some adult children use TV or scrolling the internet to completely numb out from their feelings.
name: numb out
synonyms: use a substance or behavior to severely dull your ability to feel

definition: Completely desensitized to physical and/or emotional sensations, as a result of trauma or a stimulus such as a drug.
usage_example: As a result of the constant abuse at home, I eventually became a totally numbed-out child.
name: numbed-out

definition: The state of being unable to feel emotions, or the full range of human emotions and/or physical sensations. This occurs when feelings and sensations have become “frozen”, which is an unconscious defense mechanism against abuse and neglect in the dysfunctional home.
usage_example: The numbing I experienced as a child was my brain’s response to abandonment and abuse - it kept me safe from unbearable pain.
name: numbing

definition: An adjective describing any substance or behavior that can dull or deaden physical and/or emotional sensations.
usage_example: As a young child, I discovered that eating a lot of food, especially sweet or starchy food, had a temporary numbing effect on my emotional pain.
name: numbing

definition: A partial to complete lack of physical and/or emotional feeling.
usage_example: When I feel shame, I often experience a sudden numbness in my hands and feet which makes it hard to physically move.
name: numbness

definition: Care for, feed, and protect someone or something while they are growing. Nurturing a child includes more than just caring for their physical needs. It also requires providing support and healthy growth opportunities for their intellectual, emotional, and spiritual development.
usage_example: While my parents gave sufficient attention to my physical and intellectual development, they lacked the capacity to nurture me emotionally or spiritually.
name: nurture
synonyms: encouraging and supporting the healthy development of someone or something

definition:
A reflexive pronoun which refers back to the subject of a sentence. It is used to replace the pronouns herself or himself, in situations where the speaker/writer does not want to assign gender to the subject. It can also be used in more formal language to refer back to the speaker. In this case it replaces the pronoun myself. This pronoun is also sometimes used to emphasize that the subject did something alone, without the help of others.
*In the past, one’s self and oneself were sometimes both used to mean the gender-neutral, third person reflexive pronoun (see usage example sentence). However, in Standard modern English, one’s self and oneself are two different words, with different meanings. According to the context, the writers of the Big Red Book most likely intended to use the word one’s self as a reflexive pronoun, which is now usually written as one word - oneself. When translating one’s self in ACA literature, it is suggested to use the standard definition of oneself as it appears in this glossary.
usage_example: An adult child learns in ACA to reparent oneself, and not always look first to other people to provide that unconditional love and support.
name: one’s self *, oneself
synonyms: myself (in cases where the speaker is referring back to their own person)

definition: Someone’s viewpoint or judgement, not necessarily based on fact or knowledge.
name: opinion

definition: A professional or expert’s advice about a particular subject
name: opinion

definition: An emotional state which exists beyond the challenge zone. In this state, recovery work is more difficult or even impossible. Overwhelm can occur for various reasons, such as tiredness, a trigger, or a general feeling that the current environment is not safe. When we find ourselves in the overwhelm zone, pausing active recovery work and taking a gentleness break, or calling another ACA member, can help.
usage_example: While working the Steps with another ACA member, a painful memory came up and went into the overwhelm zone. We took a break from the work to regain a sense of calm and safety.
name: overwhelm zone
synonyms: The point where you are emotionally unable to continue recovery work and need a break

definition: Earned the right to something, through hard work, long experience, and/or surviving difficulties. The idiom originates from the literal meaning of the phrase pay my dues, which is ‘pay the money required to join or remain in an organization, club, etc.’.
usage_example: My sisters and I feel we paid our dues growing up in a dysfunctional family, and now we believe we each seek only healthy relationships with people who can love and be responsible for themselves.
name: paid our dues
synonyms: earned a place at the table (idiom)

definition: A psychiatric diagnosis that is characterized by reoccurring, severe, and unexpected panic attacks. The main symptom is a sudden feeling of extreme terror. Physical symptoms may include rapid heart rate and breathing, chest pain, sweating, and dizziness. One of the known causes of panic disorder is childhood trauma.
usage_example: After being diagnosed with severe panic disorder, I started looking into how to heal childhood trauma, and went to my first ACA meeting.
name: panic disorder
synonyms: a psychiatric diagnosis that is characterized by reoccurring

definition:
An early ACA term used to describe the family members of an alcoholic, who are affected by the alcoholic’s behavior. They eventually take on symptoms of the disease, even if they do not drink alcohol. The para-alcoholic focuses on the wants and needs of others, primarily the alcoholic or addict in their life, rather than their own. 
* The word para-alcoholic was eventually changed to codependent.
usage_example: My mother was the alcoholic in the family and while my father did not drink, he was a para-alcoholic whose life and identity revolved around my mother’s drinking.
name: para-alcoholic*

definition: The process by which the family members of an alcoholic develop the traits of the disease (see L: Laundry List), even if they do not drink alcohol.
usage_example: The term para-alcoholism helped me finally to understand why my family was so dysfunctional, even though neither of my parents drank. They were the children of alcoholics, and they each brought their learned behavior of fear, control, and denial to their new family.
name: para-alcoholism

definition: A dysfunctional family situation in which a child or teenager is forced to take age-inappropriate, parental responsibilities. These tasks may be cooking, cleaning, looking after the younger children, or paying bills. Parentification may also mean the child or teenager is the main source of emotional support for a parent and/or other members of the family. At the same time, they may not receive any emotional support for themselves. It is a form of abuse and can cause childhood trauma.
usage_example: Parentification in my family took different forms: because of my mother’s depression, she wasn’t always able to cook or clean the house, and so I learned to do that by age 8 or 9. I also was the person she complained to about her problems with my father and her complicated emotions.
name: parentification
synonyms: a child/teenager taking on the responsibilities of the parent

definition: An adjective describing a child who has taken on age-inappropriate, parental responsibilities in their family. This happens when the adults in the family are physically and/or emotionally incapable of fulfilling all of their parental responsibilities.
usage_example: Parentified children, because they had to take on too much responsibility too early, often grow into adults who find it hard to relax and have fun.
name: parentified
synonyms: forced into age-inappropriate parental responsibilities (as a child/teenager)

definition: One piece of the different aspects that make up the adult child. These different pieces could be, for example, our thoughts, our feelings, and our bodies. It can also refer to different inner family members, for example, the inner child, inner teenager, the critical and the loving parent.
usage_example: I understand ACA recovery to mean a reunion of the different parts of ourselves.
name: part of ourselves

definition: A type of behavior in which a person expresses their anger, dissatisfaction, unhappiness, or their needs and wants in an indirect manner, not through direct communication. It is a form of manipulation.
usage_example: My passive-aggressive brother often stops speaking to me when he’s unhappy with something I did, instead of telling me what his problem is.
name: passive-aggressive
synonyms: indirectly expressive of anger and dissatisfaction

definition:
Someone who prioritizes other people’s needs, feelings, and opinions above their own, to avoid conflict or being abandoned.
criticism.
usage_example: I learned early in childhood to be a people-pleaser, because always agreeing with my mother and not having my own opinions or feelings helped keep me safe.
name: people-pleaser

definition: A person who has committed a violent, abusive, and/or criminal act.
usage_example: The main perpetrator in my family was my father, who physically and emotionally abused his wife and children.
name: perpetrator

definition: Existing and noticeable everywhere. Spreading from one area or thing to another. This adjective is generally used to describe something negative and unwanted.
usage_example: The effects of growing up in a dysfunctional home are pervasive. I now see how the dysfunction has spread to every aspect of my life.
name: pervasive

definition: A mental health diagnosis, also known by the abbreviation PTSD. It is caused by experiencing or witnessing a terrifying event/ events. Abuse and neglect can cause PTSD. Symptoms may include intrusive thoughts about the event(s), severe anxiety, flashbacks, nightmares, hypervigilance, and avoidance of people and places that trigger these symptoms. Feelings of anger, hopelessness, guilt, and shame are also common. PTSD in childhood interferes with normal development, creating more complex damage. Some professionals use the term complex PTSD, or cPTSD, to describe the effects of repeated, ongoing trauma, as opposed that of one traumatic event.
usage_example: In the past, people thought that only war veterans suffered from Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. It is now understood that survivors of childhood trauma, including emotional abuse, share most of the same PTSD symptoms experienced by soldiers.
name: Post Traumatic Stress Disorder/PTSD
synonyms: a psychiatric diagnosis of symptoms caused by trauma

definition: The positive quality of being of great value, loved, and cherished.
usage_example: ACA recovery and a connection with my higher power is showing me that I have a preciousness that cannot be destroyed by trauma and abuse.
name: preciousness

definition: A person who has a pattern of alcohol use that creates negative consequences in their life, for example relationship, work, or legal problems. The difference between this term and alcoholic is that an alcoholic is defined as being addicted to alcohol, where a problem drinker is not.
usage_example: Before recovery, I numbed my pain with numerous substances and behaviors: food, shopping, watching endless hours of TV. I was also a problem drinker, although I was not physically addicted to alcohol.
name: problem drinker

definition: The dysfunctional caregiver(s) whose behavior caused us to develop the Laundry List traits. It is “the person who infected us with the disease of alcoholism or dysfunction.” BRB p. 417
name: qualifier
synonyms: the person whose behavior caused us to become adult children

definition: A second word or sentence which changes the meaning of the word or sentence before it.
name: qualifier

definition: To qualify for a program or group means ‘meet a specific set of requirements necessary to be a member of that group’. To qualify for ACA specifically means you identify with/exhibit the Laundry List traits. This can be a result of growing up in a dysfunctional family or system, or otherwise experiencing childhood trauma and loss.
usage_example: All my siblings, as well as my parents, qualify for ACA. We all lived in the same abusive, dysfunctional family and it shows in our behavior.
name: qualify for ACA
synonyms: identify with/exhibit the Laundry List traits

definition: Revealed or explained something that was previously a secret.
usage_example: When I learned the details of my mother’s abusive childhood, it raised the veil on her own dysfunctional behavior with me. She was repeating what she had been taught by her dysfunctional parents.
name: raised the veil

definition: People who automatically respond, or react, to adult situations with the Laundry List traits. In this mindset, adult children often feel powerless to do anything, in other words to consciously act, about the problems in our lives. We remain dependent on other people, because their behavior determines how we feel and what we do.
usage_example: Reactors rather than actors in my life means that in a disagreement with a colleague, I automatically overreact with an angry outburst, instead of having the chance to calmly decide what a healthy action might be.
name: reactors rather than actors

definition: In general English, this means the process of becoming healthy again after a disease or injury. In ACA specifically, it means the process of healing from the emotional and spiritual wounds caused by the disease of family dysfunction. Aspects of ACA recovery include coming out of denial and isolation, reconnecting with the inner family members, grieving the losses of a traumatic childhood, and learning to reparent ourselves.
usage_example: Recovery in ACA is slow, because it means healing deep wounds, as well as learning a different way of living from what we were taught from our family of origin over many years.
name: recovery

definition: Relating to the process of healing.
usage_example: My recovery process has not been a straight line. I have had ups and downs, and sometimes I felt like I was going backwards. My sponsor tells me this is completely normal.
name: recovery

definition: An activity that is done for pleasure, in your free time.
name: recreation

definition: The act of making something happen again. Sometimes written as re-creation.
name: recreation

definition: A return to sickness or unhealthy behavior.
usage_example: My relapse started when I got into a new relationship and stopped working my ACA program.
name: relapse

definition: Return to unhealthy behavior, such as addictions and/other forms of self-harm and reliance on the Laundry List traits.
usage_example: Because I know it is easier to relapse when I isolate, I attend meetings regularly and call a fellow traveler at least twice a week to talk honestly about how I am feeling.
name: relapse

definition: Describe a series of events, tell a story
usage_example: ACA meetings were the first time in my life I felt safe enough to relate some of the details of my childhood trauma.
name: relate

definition: Identify with and understand someone or something because you have similar experiences, feelings and/or thoughts.
name: relate to

definition: Be connected with something.
name: relate to

definition: Interact with someone or something
name: relate to

definition: The use of someone’s religious or spiritual beliefs in a way that causes them harm. This includes emotional, physical, and sexual abuse that occurs within religious or spiritual communities. However, emotional, physical, and sexual religious abuse can also happen within families, when a parent, partner, or other relative uses religious or spiritual beliefs as justification to control, shame, or otherwise cause harm to their family members.
usage_example: One of the examples of emotional religious abuse in my family was using the image of an angry, frightening god to control the children.
name: religious abuse
synonyms: using someone’s religious or spiritual beliefs to harm them

definition: Trust and have faith in someone or something.
name: rely on

definition: Need a particular person or thing to function properly.
name: rely on

definition: Change the way you think about something.
usage_example: ACA is helping me to reframe my childhood, and see it for how lonely and frightening it really was.
name: reframe

definition: Giving ourselves the unconditional love, protection, nurturing, support, and guidance that our caregivers did not give us in childhood. Literally, reparenting means ‘parenting again’ (from the Greek re for ‘back’ or ‘again’). It is a process which begins with rediscovering the love inside us, which many adult children freely give to others, but not themselves. We learn to replace the harsh judgement of the inner critical parent with the love and understanding of a loving parent.
usage_example: Reparenting is giving myself all the love, nurturing, guidance, and support I wish I had received from my own parents.
name: reparenting
see_also: becoming your own loving parent. L: loving parent

definition: A specific exercise in the Loving Parent Guidebook, similar to a guided meditation. The process follows four distinct steps. The aim of the exercise is to connect with your inner family members, in particular those who may be triggered and need comfort.
usage_example: When I felt triggered by a confrontation at work, I called my ACA friend and we went through the reparenting check-in together.
name: reparenting check-in

definition: A person who feels compelled to help others, often at the expense of their own well-being. They often have the false belief that they are responsible for, and capable of, saving other people from whatever problems they have. Rescuing behavior can provide them with a sense of self-esteem, as well as a sense of control.
usage_example: Rescuers not only try to save their friends and family, but are often attracted to helping profession roles like social worker, nurse, or teacher.
name: rescuer

definition: Bitterness and indignation at having been treated badly, unfairly, or forced to accept something you do not like.
usage_example: I am learning to be honest when I don’t want to do something, instead of agreeing, but then holding resentment against the person who asked me for help.
name: resentment

definition: Having a healthy mind, being mentally well. No longer a medical term.
name: sane

definition: Reasonable, rational, displaying good judgment.
name: sane

definition: Good mental health, soundness of mind.
usage_example: Sanity for me is knowing and doing what is truly best for my own health and well-being.
name: sanity

definition: A person who is blamed incorrectly for the mistakes, bad acts, or dysfunction of others. It is one of the dysfunctional family roles. The child in this role helps the family maintain denial about their sickness, because all problems are blamed on the one child, rather than the dysfunctional parents or the family system as a whole. The scapegoated child may come to believe they truly are at fault for all the family problems.
usage_example: While my parents ignored brother’s mistakes and misbehavior, I was the family scapegoat and got blamed for anything that went wrong in the house.
name: scapegoat
synonyms: person who takes the blame for others

definition: The phenomenon, often unconscious, when a person compromises their own inner desires, beliefs, and understanding of reality.  They do this to conform to what other people want or consider acceptable. It is often a trauma response, formed during a dysfunctional childhood. In this situation, a child may learn that hiding their true feelings beliefs is a way to stay safe.
usage_example: Self-betrayal was when I chose a profession I didn’t enjoy and married someone I didn’t want to, because that was what my parents told me to do.
name: self-betrayal

definition: A psychological phenomenon in which a person feels personally and overly responsible for real or imagined problems and negative outcomes. It can come from growing up in a dysfunctional family. A child may try to make sense of their parents’ dysfunction by believing that they, the child, are the problem. This false belief is often carried into adulthood and applied to other areas of life.
usage_example: If a random person leaves and ACA meeting early, my self-blame immediately has me thinking I said or did something wrong to upset that person.
name: self-blame
synonyms: overdeveloped sense of responsibility for problems and negative outcomes

definition: The act or habit of harshly criticizing your behavior and actions as wrong, without any compassion or forgiveness for mistakes or wrongdoings.
usage_example: When I first realized I had repeated some of the dysfunctional behavior I learned from my parents, I felt a strong sense of self-condemnation. However, working an ACA program taught me how to forgive myself for my past mistakes.
name: self-condemnation

definition: A positive belief in your own abilities, qualities, and judgement.
usage_example: Keeping a daily journal of the progress I am making in ACA has given me much more self-confidence in my life.
name: self-confidence

definition: The feeling of having no confidence in yourself and your abilities. Adult children’s self-doubt can also extend to questioning our own sense of reality or truth. This is because as children in the dysfunctional home, we may have had our feelings and observations contradicted by our caregivers, who were in denial.
usage_example: My parents set extremely high standards for their children’s behavior and performance, which were impossible to meet most of the time. As a result, I grew up with a sense of permanent self-doubt that I could ever do anything successfully.
name: self-doubt

definition: The overall sense of your own value or worth.
usage_example: I was constantly criticized by my parents as a child, and developed a very low self-esteem as a result.
name: self-esteem

definition: Injury that we do to ourselves. It is conventionally understood as deliberate acts of physical injury to a person’s own body. However, ACA considers all harmful behavior the adult child may consciously or unconsciously engage in as self-harm. Examples include drug and alcohol abuse, using food to numb feelings, isolating, and people-pleasing.
usage_example: I engaged in many forms of self-harm before recovery, for example deliberately hurting myself physically, criticizing myself harshly, and isolating from people.
name: self-harm

definition: Extreme dislike of yourself, usually consisting of constant feelings of inadequacy, guilt, and low self-esteem.
usage_example: Connection with my higher power and developing an inner loving parent are transforming my self-hate into self-love.
name: self-hate

definition: Books, organizations, and programs that offer information on how to help yourself change or grow, without seeking outside professional help.
usage_example: The self-help shelf in my local bookstore is full of titles that promise I can be happier, healthier, or have more money in life.
name: self-help

definition: What adult children do in ACA Step Four. We name the acts of abandonment, shame, neglect, and other abuse we experienced as children from our dysfunctional parents. We also identify and take ownership of our adult defects of character and other dysfunctional or abusive behavior.
usage_example: Doing my self-inventory in Step Four was very healing, because it was the first time I was able to safely name the abuse and dysfunction that harmed me as a child.
name: self-inventory
synonyms: personal list of dysfunction and abuse experienced in childhood
as well as our adult character defects and dysfunctional or abusive behavior.

definition: Caring only about yourself, without concern for the needs and feelings of other people.
usage_example: My parents often shamed me as selfish for expressing certain needs and feelings, not understanding these needs were completely normal for a child of my age.
name: selfish

definition: Caring for the well-being of someone or something without needing to benefit from it personally.
usage_example: Healthy service in ACA is done for selfless reasons, because you want to support the program and bring the message to other adult children.
name: selfless

definition: The state of accepting yourself fully, treating yourself with kindness and respect, and nurturing your own well-being.
usage_example: Self-love is one of the ultimate goals of my ACA recovery program.
name: self-love
synonyms: unconditional love and acceptance for yourself

definition: The state of dwelling or being stuck in your own suffering and negative feelings, without a focus on the possibility to heal or change. A situation in which you feel you are the powerless victim, and are often unable to see a workable solution.
usage_example: When I came to ACA, I was often stuck in self-pity, because I did not believe there was a solution to the pain of childhood trauma. However, working the program has taught me I can change my thought patterns and reactions and live a better life.
name: self-pity
synonyms: stuck in the problem rather than the solution

definition: Not needing help or support from other people.
usage_example: As a child in a dysfunctional family, I had to be self-reliant in order to survive, because my alcoholic parents were often not there to prepare food or help me with schoolwork.
name: self-reliant

definition: Believing you are a more moral and generally a better person than others, and judging them harshly.
usage_example: In my self-righteous family, we acted like we were better than other people who were different from us, but secretly we were all filled with self-hate and shame.
name: self-righteous

definition: The sense that you are a good person, deserving of love and respect.
usage_example: I believe self-worth is something all people are born with, but it needs to be supported with consistent healthy, loving behavior from our family.
name: self-worth

definition: The order in which we achieve recovery as adult children. It may be different for different people, depending on the recovery path they choose. It often follows the ACA Twelve Steps.
usage_example: Many adult children say hitting bottom was the first step in their sequence of recovery, and what led them to seek help in ACA.
name: sequence of recovery
synonyms: the order in which we achieve recovery

definition: The progressive nature of the Twelve Steps, and what each step is meant to bring to the adult child working them. One through Three leads us from admitting we are powerless, to understanding the spiritual nature of recovery. Four and Five are about honest self-examination and sharing this with another person. Steps Six, Seven, and Eight are the removal of our dysfunctional behaviors and making amends to those we have harmed, including ourselves. The remaining Steps are about carrying the message to other adult children still suffering. The order in which the Steps progress is important, because they build on each other.
usage_example: The sequence of the Steps is important, because I needed the support of my higher power from Steps Two and Three to support me in Steps Four and Five.
name: sequence of the Steps
synonyms: the progressive order of the Twelve Steps

definition: The framework for how all service in ACA is organized, for example: chairing a meeting, renting a meeting space, and publishing literature. It works as a replacement for government. The shape of the ACA service structure is an inverted pyramid, with the group conscience at group level at the top. The next level down is intergroups, then service boards and committees, and at the bottom, the WSO.
usage_example: The ACA service structure consists mostly of volunteers.
name: service structure

definition: The particular place or environment where something happens.
name: setting

definition: The speed, height, or temperature at which a machine can be adjusted.
name: setting

definition: A very strong, emotional, and often physical reaction to something that causes us to feel shame. It may include regressing in age emotionally to the time of an original shaming event in our childhood. Shame attacks can lead to full takeovers (see T: takeover).
usage_example: When my boss criticized my work on the project, I found myself going into a full shame attack in her office.
name: shame attack
synonyms: strong emotional and physical reaction caused by shame

definition: Anything that removes shame. In ACA literature specifically, shame buster refers to Step Four. This Step brings us the clarity that we are not bad or shameful because of what has happened to us, or because of things we may have done.
usage_example: ACA meetings were for me the first shame busters, even before I started working on my Step Four. Hearing other adult children describe situations and feelings just like mine, I realized I was not some monster who deserved all these bad things that happened to me.
name: shame buster

definition: A dose of shame, which some adult children may be addicted to and therefore seek out unconsciously. Because adult children grew up feeling shame, it can feel familiar and comfortable, despite being painful.
usage_example: I noticed in early recovery that a shame hit made me feel safe, because it was more familiar to me than believing I was worthy and good.
name: shame hit
synonyms: dose of the shame you are addicted to

definition: Affected by physical, mental, or spiritual illness or disease. In the ACA literature, this word refers to the disease of family dysfunction, including alcoholism and other addictions.
usage_example: While only a few members of my family are alcoholics or addicts, we are all sick in some way, because family dysfunction affects everyone.
name: sick
synonyms: dysfunctional (when the disease is the disease of family dysfunction)

definition: A deep emotional wound from childhood, the damage to the mind and spirit (and potentially body) of an adult child who suffered consistent abandonment from their caregivers.
usage_example: My soul rupture means I feel extreme fear and emotional pain when I think there might be a problem in my friendships or other relationships.
name: soul rupture

definition: Relating to the human soul/spirit/inner self. Usually involves a sense of connection to something bigger than ourselves. To be spiritual, in other words focused on the human soul and its greater purpose, you do not need to belong to a particular religion or follow their specific practices.
usage_example: I understand ACA to be a spiritual program, because it teaches me how to heal my wounded soul through love for myself and others, and a connection to a power greater than myself.
name: spiritual

definition: The use of someone’s religious or spiritual beliefs in a way that causes them harm. This includes emotional, physical, and sexual abuse that occurs within religious or spiritual communities. However, emotional, physical, and sexual spiritual abuse also happens within families, when a parent, partner, or other relative uses religious or spiritual beliefs as justification to control, shame, or otherwise cause harm to their family members.
usage_example: A child being shamed or punished when they express a belief in god is spiritual abuse.
name: spiritual abuse

definition: Reveal a secret.
usage_example: The first time I ever felt safe enough to spill the beans about my abusive childhood was in an ACA meeting.
name: spill the beans
synonyms: let the cat out of the bag (idiom)

definition: A person working their Steps and/or general ACA program with a sponsor guiding them.
usage_example: As a sponsor, I continue my healing every time I share my experience, strength, and hope with one of my ACA sponsees.
name: sponsee
synonyms: fellow traveler being guided by a sponsor

definition: A person who regularly attends ACA meetings, works an active program, and is willing to be available to guide another person through the Steps. A sponsor typically has more time and experience in ACA, and has completed the Steps. However, a difference to other 12 Step groups is that an ACA sponsor and sponsee are seen as equals, rather than in a teacher-student relationship. They generally do not give advice or tell the sponsee what to do. They actively listen, reflect back what they are hearing, help present healthy alternatives to dysfunction, and share what they did in similar situations. Being a sponsor is an important part of later recovery, where we continue our own spiritual growth by guiding another person through the earlier stages of recovery.
usage_example: My sponsor guided me through the Twelve Steps, sharing their own experience, strength, and hope.
name: sponsor

definition: A relationship in which a member of the program guides another through the ACA Twelve Steps and aspects of basic recovery. In ACA, it is a partnership of equals, not a teacher-student relationship. This is a difference to other 12 Step programs. A peer-to-peer relationship works better for adult children, because they often struggle with authority figures.
usage_example: Sponsorship is beneficial to both people in the relationship. One person receives guidance and support from someone with more experience in ACA, while the other person strengthens their own recovery by sharing what they have learned.
name: sponsorship

definition: Speak or act in support of someone.
usage_example: As a child, I don’t remember ever having my parents stand up for me – everything was always my fault. As an adult in recovery, I am learning that first I need to learn how to stand up for myself.
name: stand up for

definition: Actively defend yourself or someone/something against attack or unfair circumstances.
usage_example: In ACA I am learning how to appropriately stand up to dysfunctional people when it is appropriate. I don’t explode in anger, but try to calmly and firmly state my feelings and boundaries.
name: stand up to

definition: To be fixed in a particular place or situation, unable to move or change.
usage_example: When I came to ACA, I was stuck in my unhealthy behaviors, because I had no idea how to change them. Reparenting and working the Twelve Steps is finally helping me alter my negative patterns.
name: stuck

definition: Feelings of loss and abandonment, as a result of childhood trauma, neglect, and abuse. We were unable to safely express these emotions as children in a dysfunctional family, so they stayed with us. While me may have the memory of the specific events that resulted in loss, the accompanying emotions are trapped behind denial, fear, and our own defense mechanisms. These keep us numb and disconnected from our true emotions. Stuck grief remains with us, sometimes making itself known as physical pain, illness, and/or depression, until we arrive in a safe space such as ACA. There we can finally feel the feelings and release them as they arrive.
usage_example: I released a lot of stuck grief when I did my Step Four trauma and abandonment inventories.
name: stuck grief
synonyms: repressed feelings of loss and abandonment

definition: In English we often say we are stuffed when we have eaten so much food that our stomachs are uncomfortably full. Stuffing feelings can be understood in a similar way. When we are afraid to feel our emotions openly, we repress them, or figuratively speaking, we swallow them. They do not go away, but remain inside us, causing discomfort of some kind until we eventually release them.
usage_example: I was an expert in the ability to stuff feelings for much of my life. No matter what was going on around me, I had a smile on my face. But on the inside, I was getting more and more full of all the years of repressed fear, sadness, and anger.
name: stuff feelings

definition: A person who regularly uses alcohol and/or drugs of any kind to numb emotional pain.  This term is used separately from that of addict, as a substance abuser may or may not have a physical or psychological addiction.
usage_example: Although I never became physically addicted to anything, before recovery I was a regular substance abuser. I used alcohol, drugs, and food to numb the pain I felt all the time.
name: substance abuser

definition: The uncontrolled use of alcohol and/or any kind of drug. The official medical diagnosis of substance abuse has now been changed to Substance use disorder. It is distinct from the term addiction, because it does not attempt to define whether or not physical or psychological addiction is present.
usage_example: Many adult children turn to substance abuse to numb the grief caused by growing up in a dysfunctional family.
name: substance abuse

definition: A group of people who organize around a common problem or experience, and provide each other with comfort, encouragement, and help.
usage_example: I find support groups a helpful addition to therapy, because they give me a chance to interact with other people who understand my issues.
name: support group
synonyms: 12 Step group (for groups following the Twelve Steps)

definition: A state of mind in which you feel confident and trust in your ability to do something.
usage_example: When I first started ACA, I felt very awkward and uncomfortable sharing in meetings. After a few months, however, I can now speak with sureness of foot.
name: sureness of foot

definition: The state of continuing to exist, especially despite difficult circumstances.
usage_example: I was in a state of survival for many years, but ACA is helping me move on to actually enjoying my life, not just protecting it.
name: survival

definition: Something that helps a person or thing stay alive, especially in difficult or dangerous circumstance.
usage_example: Survival skills include knowing how to protect your body in a dangerous situation, but they can also include knowing how to protect your soul in a dysfunctional family.
name: survival

definition: Another name for the Laundry List traits. Fear-and-shame-based characteristics that the adult child was forced to develop in order to survive growing up in a dysfunctional family. The Laundry List and the Other Laundry List each describe 14 specific survival traits adult children have in common, which kept us safe by making us people pleasers, invisible, and submissive. Or, in terms of the Other Laundry List, by becoming victimizers ourselves. These traits also represent the internalization of our parents’/caregivers’ behavior.
usage_example: My survival traits, such as isolating myself and people-pleasing, kept me relatively safe from the dysfunction and abuse as a child. However, as an adult they are stopping me from living a full life and having healthy, meaningful relationships.
name: survival traits/survival Traits

definition: The action of giving your power and control to someone or something.
usage_example: Surrender for many adult children means finally asking for help.
name: surrender

definition: Give up your power and control to someone and/or something else.
usage_example: Part of daily recovery for me is remembering to surrender other people’s behavior to my higher power, because I can only change myself.
name: surrender

definition: Stay alive, especially despite dangerous or difficult situations.
usage_example: In order to survive physically, children of alcoholics and/or dysfunctional families often have to shut down emotionally.
name: survive

definition: A 12 Step program phrase which means focusing on ourselves, our own issues and faults, rather than on other people and their actions and faults. Figuratively speaking, my side of the street is my responsibility alone to keep clean and tidy. Your side of the street is your responsibility to keep clean, not mine.
usage_example: When making amends to others, it is important for us to keep sweeping off our side of the street, rather than commenting on the behavior of the other person.
name: sweeping off our side of the street

definition: Stop the activity you are doing and rest for a moment.
usage_example: When my Step work becomes too overwhelming, I take a breather and do something calming like take a walk or play with my dog.
name: take a breather

definition: Do something decisively to solve a problem or achieve a goal.
usage_example: The more I take action in recovery, rather than just waiting for something to happen, the more growth I achieve.
name: take action

definition: A situation when we are deeply triggered, and the inner family member who experienced the original trauma takes over control of our adult conscious thinking and action.
usage_example: When someone took the parking space I wanted, I became so angry that I screamed at the person and hit my car. I totally overreacted, and understood later it was because I was in a takeover from my angry inner teen.
name: takeover
synonyms: A situation in which an inner family member temporarily takes control of our consciousness.

definition: Deeply afraid of being rejected and alone in life. A child’s survival is dependent on the presence of their caregivers to provide food, shelter, love, and care. As adult children we did not receive all that we needed in childhood, so this deep fear of being rejected and left alone stays with us.
usage_example: Because I am terrified of abandonment, I have stayed in some very unhealthy relationships as an adult, simply to avoid being alone.
name: terrified of abandonment
synonyms: deeply afraid of rejection and being alone

definition: A particular characteristic or quality of a person that can influence their behavior. When Trait is spelled with a capital T in the ACA literature, it refers specifically to the 14 Laundry List and Other Laundry List traits.
usage_example: In recovery I have learned that I have positive traits like empathy and resilience, as well as the adult child Traits that now affect my life negatively.
name: trait/Trait

definition: Unable to stop looking at or participating in something, because it is so interesting or compelling.
usage_example: In the past I was transfixed by other people’s drama and gossip because it was a way to avoid looking at my own issues.
name: transfixed

definition: A sight, smell, sound, thought, feeling, or action that causes a strong, sometimes overwhelming reaction because it reminds us of a past trauma. We may feel fear, shame, sadness, anxiety, anger, or a combination of these emotions. This is because the trigger returns us temporarily to the emotional state of the original trauma.
usage_example: Being criticized is a big trigger for me.  I immediately feel like a shamed, 4-year-old child. Other triggers include the smell of alcohol, and hearing people arguing.
name: trigger
synonyms: stimulus for strong emotions associated with a past trauma
catalyst for strong emotions associated with a past trauma

definition: Cause strong, sometimes overwhelming reactions of fear, sadness, anxiety, and/or anger because it reminds us of a past trauma.
usage_example: Being interrupted when I am speaking can trigger my inner teenager’s anger, but I am learning to take a deep breath when it happens and pause before acting out those feelings.
name: trigger
synonyms: activate strong emotions associated with a past trauma

definition: Having problems or difficulties.
name: troubled

definition: Feeling distressed, anxious.
name: troubled

definition: The original person, being, or soul that we were born as. This part of us knows how to love and trust. For adult children, the true self was forced into hiding in the subconscious, to protect itself from the shame, abandonment, and fear that comes from family dysfunction. A false self of Laundry List traits, addictive behaviors, and codependency took its place. The goal of recovery is to bring the true self out of hiding and reconnect with it. Some ACA members believe the true self is the inner child.
usage_example: Through ACA recovery I am slowing reconnecting with my true self. For me that means being able to feel all my feelings without judgement or fear, and learning what I actually like and don’t like, rather than doing what other people expect from me.
name: true self/True Self

definition: Someone or something that is deserving of our trust, because they are truthful, dependable, and safe.
usage_example: My ACA sponsor was one of the first trustworthy people I met in recovery; she was honest and open about her thoughts and feelings, and always did what she said she would do.
name: trustworthy

definition: Give control or responsibility over something to my higher power.
usage_example: If I feel overwhelmed by fear or anger, I get a lot of relief when turn things over to my higher power and say “I can’t do this alone.”.
name: turn things over to my higher power
synonyms: relinquish things to my higher power
let go of something and give it to my higher power

definition: The public part of the divided self, that must exist out in the world. The unfeeling self fights to remain detached from emotions and vulnerability.
usage_example: My unfeeling self allowed me to appear very successful and confident in the business world, but home alone I felt like a frightened, anxious child.
name: unfeeling self
see_also: divided self and F: feeling self

definition: The quality of thinking about what is good for other people, not only what is good for you.
usage_example: ACA has taught me that it is possible to both look after my own needs, as well as be an unselfish person who helps others when I can.
name: unselfish

definition: The treatment and teaching that a child receives from their parents/caregivers.
usage_example: Even if the details of our childhoods are different, adult children can relate to each other because we all had a dysfunctional upbringing.
name: upbringing
synonyms: the way a child is raised

definition: A more formal way to say ‘on me’.
usage_example: Before recovery, I constantly felt a heavy pressure and sadness weighing upon me.
name: upon me

definition: A person who is killed, injured, or otherwise suffers from the actions of another person, or a situation in which they have no control.
usage_example: As a child I was a victim of the abuse and dysfunction in my family, but as an adult I have control over my actions and choices. This recognition was an important step in my recovery.
name: victim

definition: Harm someone physically and/or emotionally.
usage_example: I was victimized as a child by abusive adults, but as an adult I can victimize myself with dysfunctional, self-harming behavior.
name: victimize

definition: Someone who harms or mistreats another person.
usage_example: An important step in my ACA recovery was accepting that I can also be a victimizer, lashing out cruelly at my family or coworkers when I feel challenged or unheard.
name: victimizer

definition: A point in recovery when a person struggles to move beyond seeing themselves as a victim. In this mindset, the adult child feels full of shame and unable to be helped and healed.
usage_example: Doing an honest Fourth and Fifth Step and giving my shame over to my higher power helped me move out of the victim plateau.
name: victim plateau
synonyms: being stuck in the victim mindset

definition: An adult child mindset where we wrongly see ourselves as permanent victims, unable to have any effect on the negative things that happen in life. There is also often a lack of self-accountability, where we don’t see our own role in the problem.
usage_example: Adults stuck in the victim posture still see themselves as the helpless children they were when they lived with their dysfunctional caregivers.
name: victim posture

definition: A sense of shame and self-consciousness that comes from hearing ourselves speak.
usage_example: Voice-shame caused me to fear speaking in ACA meetings, but over time I found the confidence to tell my story.
name: voice-shame
synonyms: shame we feel when hearing ourselves speak

definition: Behave in a cautious manner, so you do not upset or offend someone.
usage_example: As children, we all had to walk on eggshells around my angry father. We were careful about what we said and how we said it, because he could easily erupt in a rage at the smallest thing.
name: walk on eggshells

definition: People who have been damaged emotionally. People whose wounds you cannot see, so they may appear healthy.
usage_example: When I was younger, I was one of the walking wounded; I appeared normal and successful to the world, but inside I was in great pain as an untreated adult child.
name: walking wounded
synonyms: people with psychological rather than physical trauma

definition: Exhausted, extremely tired.
usage_example: I am often completely whipped after a session with my sponsor. The heavy emotional work is very exhausting.
name: whipped

definition: In a situation where others had complete power over you and you were not able to protect yourself from harm.
usage_example: Me and my siblings were completely at the mercy of my dysfunctional parents and other adults in our lives.
name: were completely at the mercy of others

definition: a period of time, most often used with the indefinite article a, as in a while.
usage_example: Recovery takes a while; it is important to try and be patient with ourselves as we heal.
name: while

definition: at the same time as
name: while

definition: a word used to show contrast or partial conflict between two facts or situations
name: while

definition: Make a decision to forgive past mistakes or problems and start again, as if these things had never happened.
usage_example: I made amends to the coworker I had argued with and we agreed to wipe the slate clean.
name: wipe the slate clean

definition: A person who works compulsively and an excessive amount. Workaholics find it difficult to stop working, even when it is having negative consequences on their health and personal life.
usage_example: A workaholic does not have a healthy work-life balance.
name: workaholic
synonyms: someone who works a lot and compulsively

definition: A book containing instruction and practical exercises about a specific study subject.
usage_example: The “Loving Parent Guidebook” is a recovery workbook with information and practical exercises on developing an inner loving parent.
name: workbook

definition: A list of 24 statements that describe typical adult child issues in the workplace. It is adapted from the original Laundry List.
usage_example: Reading the workplace laundry list helped me see I was reacting to my boss in the same way as I reacted to my abusive mother.
name: workplace laundry list
synonyms: list of typical adult child problems in the workplace

definition: The central agency for the ACA program. The WSO collects and sends out meeting information, creates and publishes ACA literature, and provides information about ACA to the general public.
usage_example: The WSO has a list on their website of all active ACA meetings around the world.
name: World Service Office/WSO
